title: 30 Minutes of Real English Conversation | Everyday English Listening Practice (A2–B1)

sentences.t: Hello and welcome back to Leo English podcast.
We're happy you're here with us for another friendly lesson on Leo English podcast.
Maybe you're having breakfast, walking somewhere, or relaxing after work.
Whatever your day looks like, there's a place for English in it.
I'm Tina.
And I'm Leo.
Today we follow a day from morning to evening.
We talk about breakfast, traveling, work, shopping, and making plans.
Listen for the main idea first.
You don't need to understand every word on your first listen.
And if you hear a useful sentence, try saying it aloud.
You can pause the video whenever you need more time.
Before we begin, please like this video and subscribe to Leo English podcast.
Let's get started.
Our ordinary day begins with a very serious question.
Where's the coffee?
How are you today, Leo?
You look cheerful, which usually means breakfast goes well.
I'm good. I had two eggs and some toast this morning.
I even leave home with matching socks, so things are looking promising.
What did you do this weekend?
Did you manage anything beyond successful sock selection?
On Saturday, I met my cousin at a cafe around 10:00.
We talked for an hour, then visited a market.
I bought three tomatoes and somehow came home with a houseplant.
Really? That's an interesting shopping list.
I visited my sister on Sunday and helped her cook lunch.
We made vegetable soup and enough rice for a small neighborhood.
Did you keep the extra food?
I like cooking once and eating twice.
It makes me feel organized without requiring much actual organization.
We shared it.
After lunch, we walked for 30 minutes and stopped at a bookstore.
I only wanted to look, but I bought a notebook.
Oh, I do that too.
I buy notebooks because each one promises a better of me.
Most of them still have beautifully empty pages.
Speaking of ordinary activities, that's what today's conversation is about.
Small details can turn a short answer into a real conversation.
I bought a plant gives us somewhere to begin.
It was good doesn't tell you why there's suddenly a tree beside my sofa.
Let's start with mornings.
What time do you usually wake up and what's the first thing you do after getting out of bed?
I usually wake up at 7:15.
First, I check the time, then I spend two minutes deciding whether the clock deserves my trust.
I get up at 6:45 on weekdays.
I open the curtains and drink some water before checking any messages on my phone.
That sounds peaceful.
I reach for my phone immediately, but sometimes a quick check becomes 15 minutes of watching someone repair an old chair.
I understand the temptation.
My morning routine feels easier when I do the same few things in a simple order.
What does routine mean exactly?
Does it mean something I do every day or does it have to happen at the same time?
A routine is your usual way of doing things.
The time can change, but the activities often follow a familiar pattern.
Then my routine includes looking for my glasses while wearing them.
It happens often enough to become an official part of the morning.
Mine includes making tea and preparing breakfast.
I usually have yogurt, fruit, and toast because they're quick and don't require much cleaning.
I prefer something warm.
Eggs are my favorite, but when I'm in a hurry, I have a banana and pretend that's a complete plan.
What makes you hurry?
Do you wake up late or do small things take longer than you expect?
Small things take longer.
I think I can shower, eat, and find my keys in 12 minutes.
Experience strongly disagrees with that idea.
I prepare my bag the night before.
It takes about 5 minutes and saves me from searching for things before leaving home.
I'll try that tonight.
Yesterday I found my keys inside my shoe, which raises several questions I'm not ready to answer.
Here's a useful sentence.
I'm running a little late.
It means you're behind your planned time, not necessarily moving quickly.
Good clarification. When I'm running late, I'm usually standing still beside the door, checking every pocket for the same missing object.
How do you get to work?
I take the bus most days because parking near our building is difficult.
I usually take the train.
The station is 10 minutes from my apartment, and the journey takes another 20 minutes.
My commute takes around 35 minutes.
Commute means the regular journey between home and work or between home and a place of study.
That's useful. My commute is longer on Fridays, but I enjoy listening to a short conversation while I travel.
Is the train crowded in the morning?
My bus has more passengers after 8:00, so I leave slightly earlier when possible.
It's crowded three or four mornings a week.
Yesterday someone's enormous backpack had more personal space than I did.
Crowded means full of people with little space available.
When the bus is crowded, I keep my bag close and avoid blocking the door.
I do that too.
I also check the station name carefully because I once missed my stop while listening to a story.
What happened afterward?
Did you get off at the next station and travel back?
Exactly. It added 20 minutes, but I learned the ending of the story.
Unfortunately, the story didn't explain how to arrive on time.
At work, I check my schedule first.
I look at meetings, choose my main task, and answer urgent messages before starting.
I usually open my email first, then another message appears, and suddenly I'm busy without remembering what I actually planned to do.
I prefer choosing one important task before opening everything.
Today I prepare a lesson outline before our meeting at 11:00.
I prefer a little conversation first.
Saying hello helps me feel ready, although my short greetings sometimes becomes a detailed discussion about lunch.
A greeting can be useful without taking the whole morning.
You can ask, how's your day going?
And listen to the answer.
And if someone says pretty busy, I can reply, anything interesting?
That gives them a chance to explain rather than ending there.
Exactly. What do you say if a colleague asks for help while you're finishing something important?
Usually one second, although I probably need five minutes.
That isn't very helpful when someone actually waits one second.
Try, could you give me five minutes?
It gives a clearer answer and helps the other person decide what to do next.
Could you give me five minutes?
I like that.
It sounds polite without requiring a long explanation about everything happening inside my computer.
Around 10:30 I take a short break.
I stand up, get water, and look away from my screen for a while.
I sometimes forget to take a break.

I keep a water bottle beside my desk as a reminder.
What helps you notice when it's time to stop briefly?
Hunger usually sends a clear message, but I can set a reminder before that, especially on days with several meetings.
Speaking of hunger, what do you usually have for lunch?
I bring food from home about four days a week.
I buy lunch twice a week and bring something on other days.
Today I have rice, chicken, and vegetables in a blue container.
I bring soup and bread today.
I like preparing a packed lunch because I don't need to choose a restaurant during my break.
Wait, what does packed lunch mean?
Does the food have to fit tightly inside the container like people on my morning train?
No, it means a meal prepared earlier and taken somewhere to eat.
It can be simple like a sandwich and fruit.
Good. My container isn't crowded, although the carrots seem extremely close to the rice.
I hope everyone gets along.
Do you eat at your desk or somewhere else?
I prefer the small kitchen because it gives me a change of place.
I agree mostly, but if it's noisy, I eat outside.
There's a quiet square 5 minutes away with three benches and some trees.
That sounds nice.
A change of place can also give you something new to discuss, like the weather or a nearby cafe.
Exactly. Yesterday a bird stood beside my bench and watched every bite.
I felt like my lunch had a very strict manager.
What happens after lunch?
I sometimes feel sleepy around two, especially when I spend the whole morning sitting down.
Oh, I do that too.
I feel low on energy after a large meal, so I try taking a short walk.
Low on energy means you feel tired and don't have much strength for activities.
It's a useful way to describe an ordinary feeling.
Then I can say I'm a little low on energy today.
It explains things better than announcing that my brain closes after lunch.
Exactly. If I still have difficult work, I divide it into smaller steps.
That makes the task feel manageable.
What does manageable mean?
I hear that word often when people give advice about busy days.
It means possible to deal with without too much difficulty.
Writing one paragraph feels more manageable than thinking about the entire unfinished report.
I understand. Cleaning one shelf feels manageable.
Cleaning my whole apartment makes me suddenly interested in visiting someone else's apartment instead.
Now let's finish work and run some errands.
I need to stop at the pharmacy and return a library book today.
Errands are small necessary trips, right?
I need to collect a package and buy washing liquid because I finished the bottle yesterday.
That's right. Since yesterday is a finished time, say I finished the bottle yesterday.
Small corrections help us describe events clearly.
I finished the bottle yesterday.
Thanks. Today I'm running errands after work, and hopefully I 'm not buying another unexpected wax plant.

what we need at home.

We ran out of bread yesterday, but somehow we still have six kinds of sauce.
Exactly. And for yesterday, say we ran out of bread.
At the shop, you can ask, excuse me, where can I find the bread?
That's useful when stores change things around.
Last week, I searched for pasta for 10 minutes and discovered I was beside pet food.
Do you usually follow a shopping list?
I write down five or six things, then check prices before putting them in my basket.
I follow a list until I see biscuits.
Then the list becomes more of a friendly suggestion than a serious document.
I buy extra things sometimes too, but I try to cut back on unnecessary purchases when I need to save money.
What does cut back on mean?
Is it stopping completely or can I still have a reasonable relationship with biscuits?
It means reducing something, not always stopping it.
You might buy one packet instead of three or order takeaway less often.
That sounds possible.
I want to cut back on food delivery because the small delivery charges become a surprisingly large amount each month.
After shopping, I head home around 6:00.
If my bags are heavy, I take the bus instead of walking.
I prefer walking when the weather is good.
It takes 20 minutes from the shop and I enjoy having no screen in front of me.
What do you do first when you arrive?
I put cold food away before changing into comfortable clothes.
I put my keys in a bowl by the door.
It's a new system and I'm trying to stop using shoes as storage.
Then I tidy up for 10 minutes.
Tidy up means putting things in their proper places, not necessarily cleaning every surface.
I like that difference.
I can tidy up the living room without deciding to wash the curtains and reorganize my entire life.
What's your usual dinner?
I often cook vegetables with rice or pasta because the ingredients are simple and easy to change.
I make eggs, soup, or a chicken sandwich.
I prefer quick meals during the week, but on Saturday I enjoy trying something new.
sometimes cook enough for two meals.
Tomorrow's lunch is ready and I have fewer things to prepare before leaving home.
That's smart. My only problem is eating tomorrow's lunch tonight because it looks particularly good beside today's dinner.
After dinner, do you prefer going out or staying in?
I usually stay in during the week because I enjoy quiet evenings.
I prefer going out once or twice a week, but tonight I'm staying in, watching one episode and watering my surprise plant.
If a friend invites you out, you can say, thanks, but I'm having a quiet night.
It's friendly and gives a simple reason.
Or could we meet on Saturday instead?
That shows I still want to see them even if my energy is low tonight.
Before bed, I prepare my clothes and check tomorrow's schedule.
Then I read for 15 minutes instead of starting another long video.
I'm trying a similar routine.
My final sentence today is, I need to get some rest, followed by actually turning the light off.
You know, Leo, while we were talking, we used many useful words.
Let's review 10 you can connect to your own daily life.
Good. I remember the biscuits clearly, but a little vocabulary review helps too.
First word, routine.
This means your usual way of doing things.
We describe our morning routines, including breakfast and preparing to leave.
So a routine can include several activities, not just one habit.
Exactly. For example, my evening routine includes reading before bed.
A habit is one repeated behavior.
And you can say, our weekend routine changes during the summer.
What's your favorite part of your routine?
I enjoy breakfast because it gives me a comfortable start.
Next word, commute.
This means a regular journey between home and work or study.
We compare our bus and train journeys.
Can it be a noun and a verb?
My commute takes 40 minutes.
You can also say I commute by bus.
And another example is she commutes to college three days a week.
What makes your commute pleasant?
I enjoy listening to conversations because the time feels useful.
Next word, crowded.
This means full of people with little space available.
We use it to describe morning public transport.
So an empty train is the opposite.
Exactly. For example, the beach is crowded on sunny weekends.
And you can say this restaurant gets crowded after 7:00.
Use crowded with people, not crowded of people.
What places do you avoid?
I avoid crowded shopping centers because I prefer walking comfortably.
Next phrase, packed lunch.
This means food prepared earlier and carried somewhere to eat.
We discuss taking lunch to work.
But it doesn't mean squeezing the food tightly together.
Exactly. For example, my daughter takes a packed lunch to school.
And you can say we bring packed lunches for our afternoon trip.
Lunch is the meal.
Packed describes its preparation.
What do you prefer packing?
I pack sandwiches because they're easy to carry and eat.
Next phrase, low on energy.
This means feeling tired or having little strength available.
We use it for our afternoon feeling.
Is it the same as feeling lazy?
Not necessarily. For example, I'm low on energy after a busy morning.
And you can say he feels low on energy and needs a break.
We also say low on milk when little remains.
What helps you?
I take a quiet break because constant conversation sometimes tires me.
Next word, manageable.
This means possible to handle without too much difficulty.
We divide large tasks into smaller steps.
So manageable doesn't always mean completely easy.
Exactly. For example, with help the extra work becomes manageable.
And you can say this short reading task feels manageable today.
Unmanageable is the opposite.
How do you make housework manageable?
I choose one room because thinking about every room feels overwhelming.
Next word, errands.
These are short trips to do necessary things.
We mention collecting packages and visiting the pharmacy.
Does going to a concert count as an errand?
Usually not. For example, I do my errands before lunch and you can say dad runs a few errands after work.
Say run errands or do errands, not make errands.
When do you do yours?
I do errands on weekdays because I prefer keeping Saturday free.
Next phrase, run out of.
This means use all of something so none remains.
We talk about milk, bread, and washing liquid.
And the past form is ran out of, right?
Exactly. For example, we ran out of printer paper this morning and you can say don't let your phone run out of battery.
Keep of before the thing that's gone.
What do you often forget?
I forget toothpaste because the tube always looks partly full.
Next phrase, cut back on.
This means reduce how much you use or do something.
We discuss spending less on deliveries.
But it doesn't always mean giving something up completely.
Exactly. For example, I want to cut back on sugary drinks and you can say we cut back on expensive trips this year.
Include on before the activity or item.
What's your personal goal?
I cut back on late shopping because tired decisions get expensive.
Final phrase,
tidy up. This means put things where they belong.
We use it for a short evening task.
So cleaning removes dirt, but tidying organizes things.
For example, please tidy up your desk before leaving.
And you can say we tidy up the kitchen after breakfast.
You can also say tidy the room.
What area needs your attention?
I tidy up my table because papers keep hiding my keys.
Here's our summary.
